items.title: World AIDS Day: People still don’t have access to key HIV prevention medicine
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

Despite generic lenacapavir slowly becoming available for some, Gilead continues to stand in the way of equitable and affordable access amid urgent global need and demand.

NEW YORK/JOHANNESBURG, NOVEMBER 26 — In advance of World AIDS Day on December 1, Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is once again calling for more people globally to have access to the highly effective HIV prevention medicine lenacapavir. This twice-yearly injectable version of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is the biggest breakthrough in HIV prevention yet, but US-based Gilead Sciences continues to block affordable access for countries around the world. This includes countries with growing HIV epidemics and ongoing humanitarian crises.

As a result of its long-acting nature, lenacapavir may be especially valuable for stigmatized or criminalized populations, who often are excluded from or concerned about accessing health care. It is also a critical tool for people on the move who may struggle to access health clinics, people living in remote areas with few health care options, and people caught in humanitarian emergencies — including those in many of the communities in which MSF operates.

“Gilead’s greed alone is the reason people across the globe don’t have access to lenacapavir already,” said Carlota Baptista da Silva, MSF’s global HIV/HCV access and advocacy lead. “Our teams are ready to provide it but have been left empty-handed or with very few doses to offer. We have patients in Eswatini and Zimbabwe ​ who’ve asked for this medicine and have been told it’s not an option because those countries' stocks had already been depleted. Kenya was supposed to see a priority roll-out but instead has faced severe shortages and delays in access. And communities where the lenacapavir clinical trials were held in Brazil, Argentina, Peru, and Mexico haven’t been guaranteed affordable access to it by Gilead.”

A generic version of this twice-yearly PrEP made by Indian manufacturer Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) in November. Dr. Reddy’s has agreed to sell its version of lenacapavir for $40 per person per year compared to the more than $28,000 per person per year that Gilead sells it for in the US. The first delivery of generics arrived in Zambia on the 25th November. However, generics won’t be available everywhere; dozens of middle-income countries will not have access to them because of the restrictive terms of Gilead’s licensing agreements.

Countries blocked from accessing generics include most of Latin America, where HIV infections rose 25 percent between 2010 and 2025. An agreement Gilead has struck with the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) to supply lenacapavir in Latin America does little to ease concerns about access; the agreement ensures Gilead’s total control over supply in the region without revealing the price it will charge. Without the availability of generic lenacapavir, people in these countries are likely to pay far more than the $40 available elsewhere.

“Even with the approval and arrival of generic lenacapavir, Gilead is still dictating which countries can access it and which cannot,” Baptista da Silva said. “The company continues to keep affordable versions of this medicine out of reach for millions by restricting which manufacturers can produce it and where they can sell it. The company could choose to expand the list of countries eligible for affordable generic versions of lenacapavir but is choosing to protect its profits instead. The only way to possibly end AIDS is to increase access to prevention tools like this one."

These access gaps come amid recent funding cuts to HIV programs by many key governments, many of which have historically funded global HIV/AIDS efforts. Prevention efforts and services, particularly those targeting stigmatized populations, have been hit the hardest.

“Many of our patients are caught in conflict, have been forced from their homes, or live in places with few health care options,” Baptista da Silva said. “Only having to get this medicine twice per year would make it much easier for someone to remain protected against HIV even if they’re on the move or unable to access a medical facility between injections. But they can only do that if it’s available more widely and affordable for them. It’s simply unacceptable that a single pharmaceutical company can dictate who can access this medicine and who can’t.”

Lenacapavir must be available for $40 or less in all low- and middle-income countries. Governments must step in to help increase access if Gilead continues to block generics from being sold in more countries.

ENDS.

items.title: World AIDS Day 2026 - Statement by Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: UNAIDS

World AIDS Day 2026 is my last as Executive Director of UNAIDS. Today, we remember the nearly 45 million people we have lost to AIDS and we stand in solidarity with the 41 million people living with HIV and with the communities who have carried this response forward with courage, determination and love.

In reflecting on the past and looking to the future, I feel both immense pride and deep concern.

Pride in what has been achieved through science, solidarity and struggle. Concern that, at the very moment when we have the tools to end AIDS, political choices and deepening inequalities threaten to put that goal beyond our reach.

Thirty years of progress, struggle and solidarity

I remember when an HIV diagnosis was effectively a death sentence. Today, 32.1 million people are receiving life-saving treatment, including 29 million in developing countries.

This extraordinary achievement represents a collective victory. A victory for people living with HIV who refused to accept that their lives were worth less than those of others. For activists who challenged the power of pharmaceutical corporations and held governments to account for realising rights. For communities who confronted prejudice and discrimination. And for governments that recognised their shared responsibility to end a global health crisis.

For decades, the AIDS movement has challenged the inequalities that drive AIDS.

Science must translate into access

Today, science has brought us to another turning point.

Lenacapavir, an HIV prevention injection administered just twice a year, could transform our ability to prevent new infections. By June of this year, more than 50,000 people in nine sub-Saharan African countries had received it. From 2027, generic versions are expected to become available at just US$40 per person per year in eligible lower-income countries. Other long-acting prevention and treatment technologies are advancing rapidly.

Imagine what these innovations could mean for adolescent girls and young women in Africa, who continue to face an unacceptable burden of new HIV infections.

But I have learned one lesson from decades of fighting inequality: a scientific breakthrough is not a public health breakthrough until it reaches the people who need it.

That is why, this World AIDS Day, our message is simple: ending AIDS starts with access.

Access is about rights and justice

Access is about more than the simple existence of a clinic or a treatment. It is about whether medicines are affordable. Whether a person living with HIV can receive treatment without stigma or discrimination Whether a young woman has the power to protect herself. Whether a gay man can seek health care without fear of arrest. Whether a sex worker can enter a clinic without humiliation. Whether activists and communities can organise and gather to protest, demand change, and achieve solidarity.

Access is about power, rights and justice.

And today, all three are under attack.

We cannot allow progress to be reversed

The global AIDS response has been shaken by a financing shock of historic proportions. International HIV assistance fell by 18% in 2025, and the annual financing gap in developing countries now stands at US$4.3 billion.

The latest UNAIDS report reveals the scale of the damage. Across countries reporting data, around 446,000 fewer people received oral HIV prevention medicines in 2025 than in 2024. Worldwide, 300 million fewer condoms were distributed. In priority countries, the number of voluntary medical male circumcisions fell by more than half.

It is unconscionable that, just as science is expanding the possibilities for HIV prevention, access to even the most established prevention tools is being eroded.

And the worst consequences of these cuts still lie ahead. Today's figures cannot yet tell us the full story of the lives that will be affected by the decisions taken over the past two years.

A young woman who fails to access prevention today may acquire HIV tomorrow. A person who loses the support they need to stay on treatment may become seriously ill in the months ahead.

We must act now, before these setbacks translate into needless HIV infections and AIDS-related deaths.

I am particularly concerned about the dismantling of community-led services. Community organisations have been among the first to lose funding, even as organised anti-rights movements are making their work more difficult and, in some places, more dangerous.

These are the organisations that have spent decades building trust with people whom health systems have too often failed. They have reached the most marginalised communities, helped people access prevention and treatment, and defended their right to health.

Once lost, that infrastructure, that knowledge, those relationships and that trust cannot easily be rebuilt.

At the same time, we are witnessing attacks on gender equality, sexual and reproductive health and rights, and the rights of LGBTQ+ people. Civic space is shrinking. Discriminatory laws and policies are driving people away from health services.

We cannot end AIDS while denying people their rights. And we cannot protect the gains of the AIDS response while dismantling the community organisations that made those gains possible.

Countries must have the means to lead

The financing crisis has forced an overdue conversation about the future of the AIDS response. I welcome the growing determination of countries to strengthen national ownership, increase domestic investment and integrate HIV services into inclusive, rights-based national health systems.

UNAIDS has recorded increases in domestic HIV expenditure in 55 countries. Those governments’ leadership deserves recognition and support.

But national ownership cannot mean abandoning international solidarity.

In many countries heavily affected by HIV, debt servicing outstrips public spending on health. This means that scarce revenues are being diverted to pay creditors while organisations are operating on the breadline and individuals are vulnerable.

We cannot expect countries to replace aid financing overnight. And we cannot demand that governments invest more in their people's health while tolerating an international financial architecture that denies them the resources to do so.

We need debt relief and fairer international financing rules. We need a planned transition away from aid, while countries build nationally owned and sustainably financed HIV responses. And we need to reform the rules governing intellectual property so that publicly supported scientific innovation serves the public good, rather than allowing monopolies and high prices to determine who lives and who dies.

These are political choices, driven by interests. But people have confronted interests and changed policies before, and will do again.

We can still end AIDS

Even in this most challenging of years, I have found reasons for hope.

Thirty years ago, UNAIDS was created because the world recognised that defeating AIDS required something different: a joint effort bringing together governments, the United Nations, scientists and communities. That model of solidarity and shared leadership has helped transform the course of the epidemic.

This year, 149 countries voted in favour of an ambitious new United Nations Political Declaration on HIV and AIDS.

Governments committed to reaching 40 million people with HIV treatment and 20 million with antiretroviral-based prevention by 2030. They committed to mobilising US$21.9 billion annually for the AIDS response in low- and middle-income countries, to defending human rights and gender equality, and to strengthening and financing community leadership.

If these commitments are fulfilled, an estimated 3.2 million new HIV infections and 1.3 million AIDS-related deaths could be averted by 2030.

On this World AIDS Day, I urge governments to make HIV a national priority, to invest in sustainable, inclusive and rights-based health systems, to remove the legal and social barriers that deny people access to services, and to ensure that communities are resourced and empowered to lead the AIDS response.

And I urge the international community to renew, rather than retreat from, its commitment to ending AIDS.

As I mark my last World AIDS Day as Executive Director of UNAIDS, I draw strength from the extraordinary courage of the AIDS movement.

Throughout my years leading UNAIDS, I have seen people living with HIV, women's movements, LGBTQ+ activists and other community leaders refuse to surrender, even in the most hostile circumstances. They have defended rights, challenged injustice and kept services alive when institutions failed them.

They remind us that progress is never inevitable. It must be fought for, and protected against backlash or weakening political will.

Ending AIDS requires political courage: to invest in people, defend human rights, confront inequality and put the public good before private profit.

The communities most affected by HIV have shown that courage for decades.

We have the science. We know what works. We know what stands in our way.

The question is no longer whether we can end AIDS. It is whether we will make the choices necessary to do so.

We must not fail this generation.

Ending AIDS starts with access.

items.title: Sudan: El Niño suma nuevos puntos críticos del hambre mientras los conflictos siguen aumentando el riesgo de hambruna, advierten la FAO y WFP
items.blurb:
Countries: Sudan, Central African Republic, Chad, Eswatini, Guatemala, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mozambique, Myanmar, Nigeria, Somalia, South Sudan, Yemen, Zambia, Zimbabwe
Sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Food Programme

Sudán, Sudán del Sur, Somalia, algunas zonas de Nigeria y Yemen siguen siendo los puntos críticos de máxima preocupación, mientras que África austral y el Corredor Seco Centroamericano figuran entre las nuevas incorporaciones.

ROMA – El Niño ha llevado a África austral y al Corredor Seco Centroamericano a la lista de puntos críticos del hambre, donde se prevé que la inseguridad alimentaria aguda empeore significativamente entre diciembre de 2026 y mayo de 2027, advirtieron hoy la Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO) y el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas (WFP). En su último informe Hunger Hotspots (Puntos críticos del hambre), los organismos también identificaron un riesgo de hambruna en algunas zonas de Sudán y Sudán del Sur.

El informe, publicado dos veces al año a través de la Red Mundial contra las Crisis Alimentarias, identifica 16 puntos críticos, frente a los 13 registrados en junio. El Niño es uno de los principales factores detrás de tres de los cuatro nuevos puntos críticos identificados: África austral (Eswatini, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia y Zimbabwe), el Corredor Seco Centroamericano y el noreste de Uganda. Chad se ha incorporado a la lista debido a los efectos persistentes del conflicto en el vecino Sudán.

El Niño está cobrando fuerza y podría convertirse en uno de los más intensos jamás registrados. En África austral, las condiciones más secas y cálidas amenazan las siembras, las labores agrícolas y las futuras cosechas. Se prevé que hasta 3 millones de personas en Zimbabwe, 2,6 millones en Malawi y 1,8 millones en Mozambique enfrenten altos niveles de inseguridad alimentaria aguda en los próximos meses, hasta marzo de 2027

En el Corredor Seco Centroamericano, la temporada de Primera de 2026 fue la más seca en cuatro décadas y las pérdidas de cultivos superaron el 75 por ciento en muchas zonas. A medida que se agotan las reservas de alimentos, la temporada de escasez de 2027 podría comenzar antes de lo habitual. Solo en Guatemala, se prevé que 3,2 millones de personas enfrenten altos niveles de inseguridad alimentaria aguda entre octubre de 2026 y febrero de 2027.

Actuar antes de que lleguen los peores efectos de El Niño puede evitar daños a las cosechas, el ganado y los medios de vida. El plan conjunto de acción anticipatoria de la FAO y WFP frente a El Niño tiene como objetivo proteger a 9 millones de personas en 22 países.

En otras regiones, los conflictos y la violencia armada siguen figurando entre los principales factores que impulsan la inseguridad alimentaria aguda en 12 de los 16 puntos críticos, incluidos los cinco puntos críticos de máxima preocupación: Sudán, Sudán del Sur, Somalia, algunas zonas de Nigeria y Yemen. En cuatro de estos cinco puntos críticos, los análisis más recientes identificaron o proyectaron poblaciones en situación de Catástrofe, la fase más grave de la Clasificación Integrada de la Seguridad Alimentaria en Fases (CIF), caracterizada por la inanición y la muerte.

En Somalia, aunque actualmente no se prevé que ninguna población enfrente una situación de Catástrofe (Fase 5 de la CIF) y el riesgo de hambruna ha disminuido, la inseguridad alimentaria aguda se mantiene en niveles de Emergencia (Fase 4 de la CIF) entre las poblaciones desplazadas en Baidoa.

Las situaciones más graves se registran en Sudán y Sudán del Sur, donde se ha identificado un riesgo de hambruna. Bajo un escenario razonable de máxima gravedad, existe riesgo de hambruna en 13 zonas de Darfur del Norte y Kordofán del Sur, en Sudán, hasta enero de 2027, mientras que en dos campamentos para personas desplazadas en Darfur del Sur los niveles de malnutrición aguda ya han superado los umbrales de hambruna. En Sudán del Sur, el último análisis disponible indicó un riesgo de hambruna en cuatro condados de los estados de Alto Nilo y Jonglei hasta julio de 2026, bajo un escenario de máxima gravedad.

Los cinco puntos críticos de máxima preocupación se han mantenido reiteradamente en este nivel desde 2022. Sin embargo, la financiación destinada a la asistencia humanitaria para la seguridad alimentaria y la nutrición en estos puntos críticos cayó un 62 por ciento, de USD 5.100 millones en 2022 a USD 2.000 millones en 2025.

Otros cuatro puntos críticos están clasificados como de muy alta preocupación: Afganistán, la República Democrática del Congo, Haití y Palestina. Aunque la seguridad alimentaria en la Franja de Gaza ha comenzado a mejorar tras el alto el fuego de octubre de 2025, los avances son frágiles y se prevé que la inseguridad alimentaria aguda empeore en Cisjordania.

La FAO y WFP hacen un llamado a adoptar medidas humanitarias urgentes en los 16 puntos críticos, sobre todo allí donde se ha identificado un riesgo de hambruna, y a garantizar un acceso seguro y sin obstáculos a las personas que necesitan asistencia.

“El Niño se está intensificando, amenazando los cultivos y las cosechas en regiones que ya son vulnerables y aumentando el riesgo de inseguridad alimentaria aguda”, afirmó el Director General de la FAO, QU Dongyu. “Sin embargo, los peores escenarios no son inevitables. La asistencia agrícola que salva vidas, destinada a impulsar la producción de alimentos de las familias altamente vulnerables, es una parte esencial de la respuesta multisectorial a las situaciones descritas en el informe. Ahí es donde la FAO está centrando sus esfuerzos”.

“He hecho un llamado a todas las naciones para desterrar la hambruna a los libros de historia”, afirmó el Director Ejecutivo de WFP, Luke J. Lindberg. “Este informe nos indica dónde podría producirse la próxima hambruna, por lo que el momento de cumplir nuestro compromiso es ahora. Será necesario un esfuerzo conjunto para poner fin a los conflictos, dotar de todos los recursos necesarios a nuestros equipos de WFP sobre el terreno y garantizar que tengan acceso seguro para llegar a las comunidades vulnerables. No se trata de un problema de capacidad operativa, sino de si los líderes mundiales tienen el valor político para actuar con decisión”.

# # #

Los 16 puntos críticos del hambre

Máxima preocupación: Sudán, Sudán del Sur, Somalia, algunas zonas de Nigeria y Yemen.

Muy alta preocupación: Afganistán, República Democrática del Congo, Haití y Palestina.

Otros puntos críticos: Chad, Corredor Seco Centroamericano, Madagascar, Malí, Myanmar, África austral (Eswatini, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia y Zimbabwe) y el noreste de Uganda.

Chad, el Corredor Seco Centroamericano, África austral y el noreste de Uganda son nuevas incorporaciones a la lista. Líbano ya no figura como punto crítico.

Nota sobre las fases de la CIF

La Fase 3 de la CIF se refiere a niveles de “Crisis” de inseguridad alimentaria, en los que los hogares presentan brechas en el consumo de alimentos que se reflejan en niveles altos o superiores a los habituales de malnutrición aguda, o apenas pueden satisfacer sus necesidades alimentarias mínimas, pero solo agotando activos esenciales para sus medios de vida o recurriendo a estrategias de afrontamiento de crisis.

La Fase 4 de la CIF se refiere a niveles de “Emergencia” de inseguridad alimentaria, en los que los hogares presentan grandes brechas en el consumo de alimentos, reflejadas en niveles muy altos de malnutrición aguda y exceso de mortalidad, o logran mitigar estas brechas únicamente mediante estrategias de emergencia relacionadas con sus medios de vida y la liquidación de activos.

La Fase 5 de la CIF se refiere a niveles de “Catástrofe/Hambruna”, en los que los hogares enfrentan una carencia extrema de alimentos y/o de otras necesidades básicas incluso después de emplear plenamente sus estrategias de afrontamiento. Son evidentes la inanición, la muerte, la indigencia y niveles extremadamente críticos de malnutrición aguda. A nivel de los hogares, la Fase 5 de la CIF se clasifica como Catástrofe, mientras que la hambruna es una clasificación a nivel de área que requiere pruebas de que se han alcanzado los umbrales de inseguridad alimentaria aguda, malnutrición aguda y mortalidad. El Cadre Harmonisé (CH), utilizado en África Occidental y el Sahel, emplea las mismas fases.

Notas para los editores

Identificados mediante análisis prospectivos, los puntos críticos del hambre son zonas donde es probable que la inseguridad alimentaria aguda se deteriore significativamente durante el período de perspectivas. Se seleccionan mediante un proceso basado en el consenso en el que participan los equipos técnicos y sobre el terreno de la FAO y WFP, junto con analistas especializados en conflictos, riesgos económicos y amenazas naturales. El informe se elabora con el apoyo financiero de la Unión Europea a través de la Red Mundial contra las Crisis Alimentarias.

El informe completo puede consultarse aquí.

El material de apoyo (B-roll) y la lista de tomas pueden consultarse aquí.

Las fotografías pueden consultarse aquí.

La Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO) es un organismo especializado que lidera los esfuerzos internacionales para acabar con el hambre. Su objetivo es lograr la seguridad alimentaria para todos y garantizar el acceso regular a suficientes alimentos de alta calidad para llevar una vida activa y saludable. La FAO trabaja en más de 130 países para transformar los sistemas agroalimentarios y hacerlos más eficientes, inclusivos, resilientes y sostenibles.

El Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas (WFP) es la organización humanitaria más grande del mundo, que salva vidas en situaciones de emergencia y utiliza la asistencia alimentaria para construir un camino hacia la paz, la estabilidad y la prosperidad para las personas que se recuperan de conflictos, desastres y los efectos de fenómenos meteorológicos extremos

items.title: World: Carte des alertes de maladies épidémiques et émergentes en Océanie - 24 novembre 2026
items.blurb:
Countries: World, Australia, French Polynesia (France), Micronesia (Federated States of), New Zealand, Papua New Guinea
Source: Pacific Community

Please refer to the attached Map.

Éléments nouveaux/faits marquants intervenus depuis la diffusion de la carte précédente sur PacNet, le 17 novembre 2026 :

Maladies diarrhéiques

• États fédérés de Micronésie (État de Yap) : D’après le bulletin hebdomadaire de l’État de Yap pour la semaine épidémiologique 46 (du 9 au 15 novembre 2026), le nombre de cas de maladies diarrhéiques a renoué avec le seuil d’alerte (7 cas), après deux semaines sous le seuil : 7 cas ont été signalés dans le service de consultation externe de l’Hôpital de l’État de Yap, contre 3 au cours de la semaine 45. Il s’agissait de 3 enfants âgés de 3 à 5 ans et de 4 adultes âgés de 36 à 64 ans. Sur les deux échantillons de selles testés, l’un s’est révélé positif au rotavirus et l’autre, à Escherichia coli entéro-agrégatif. Depuis la semaine 32, le laboratoire a détecté 137 agents pathogènes, essentiellement E. coli (59 cas) et le rotavirus (40 cas), avec des co-infections chez 67 % des cas confirmés. L’alerte bleue pour les maladies diarrhéiques est maintenue pour les États fédérés de Micronésie (État de Yap). – Source : Département de la santé de Yap, Rapport hebdomadaire sur les maladies transmissibles, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 20 novembre 2026.

Rougeole

• Papouasie-Nouvelle-Guinée : Les bulletins hebdomadaires du Département national de la santé pour les semaines épidémiologiques 45 et 46 (du 2 au 15 novembre 2026) font état d’une augmentation du nombre de cas de fièvre éruptive aiguë au niveau national : 11 cas au cours de la semaine 44, 17 au cours de la semaine 45, et 24 au cours de la semaine 46, des chiffres supérieurs à la médiane hebdomadaire habituelle. Au cours de la semaine 46, 16 cas ont été signalés dans la province du Golfe (ils viennent s’ajouter aux deux cas recensés plus tôt dans l’année), ainsi que 3 dans le district de la Capitale nationale, 2 dans les Highlands orientales, 1 à Hela, 1 à Madang et 1 à Manus. Entre le 1er janvier et la semaine 45, 505 cas ont été signalés et 460 échantillons ont été testés, dont 19 se sont révélés positifs aux anticorps IgM de la rougeole. Après examen du groupe d’experts, deux cas de rougeole (1 en Nouvelle-Irlande et 1 dans Highlands occidentales) et deux cas de rubéole restent confirmés en 2026. L’alerte bleue pour la rougeole est maintenue en Papouasie-Nouvelle-Guinée. – Source : Département national de la santé de Papouasie-Nouvelle-Guinée, Bulletin hebdomadaire sur les événements de santé publique (semaines épidémiologiques 45 et 46), communiqués au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 20 novembre 2026.

Maladies respiratoires

• Polynésie française : La Polynésie française est restée en phase épidémique pour la grippe au cours de la semaine épidémiologique 46 (du 9 au 15 novembre 2026), le nombre de cas confirmés biologiquement passant à 142, dont 139 cas de grippe A. Cinquante-six personnes ont été hospitalisées, dont 7 en réanimation. Deux décès ont été signalés. Depuis le 5 octobre (semaine 41), 427 cas confirmés (dont 372 cas de grippe A), 149 hospitalisations, 13 admissions en réanimation et 6 décès ont été recensés. Le nombre de consultations pour infection respiratoire aiguë au sein du réseau sentinelle reste stable, mais leur proportion augmente. Les autres pathogènes respiratoires détectés sont les suivants : métapneumovirus, parainfluenza 4 et rhino/entérovirus. L’alerte rouge pour la grippe A est maintenue en Polynésie française. – Source : Agence de régulation de l’action sanitaire et sociale (ARASS), Bulletin de surveillance sanitaire de Polynésie française no 41, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 24 novembre 2026.

• Nouvelle-Zélande : Le rapport hebdomadaire de virologie relatif à la semaine 46 (qui s’est achevée le 15 novembre 2026) fait état de 6 018 prélèvements positifs à la grippe depuis le 1er janvier 2026 : 5 561 cas de grippe A (992 de sous-type A(H1N1)pdm09, 880 de sous-type A(H3N2) et 3 689 non sous-typés) et 457 cas de grippe B. Ce sont 58 cas de plus qu’au cours de la semaine 45, signe que le ralentissement du nombre de détections se poursuit. L’alerte bleue pour la grippe A est maintenue en Nouvelle-Zélande. – Source : PHF Science, Rapport virologique hebdomadaire pour la Nouvelle-Zélande, page consultée le 24 novembre 2026.

Autres informations :

Entérobactéries productrices de carbapénémase

• Europe : Le 18 novembre 2026, le Centre européen de prévention et de contrôle des maladies (ECDC) a indiqué que l’incidence estimée des infections sanguines à Klebsiella pneumoniae, une bactérie productrice de carbapénémase, avait atteint 3,75 pour 100 000 habitants en 2025 dans l’Union européenne/Espace économique européen (UE/EEE). Ce taux est supérieur de 72 % au niveau de référence de 2019 et dépasse largement l’objectif 2030 (2,07 pour 100 000 habitants). L’ECDC estime que le risque est très élevé pour les personnes recevant des soins médicaux dans l’UE/EEE. La circulation de bactéries hébergeant l’enzyme New Delhi métallo-β-lactamase (NDM) augmente, avec au moins un isolat positif dans 84,3 % des territoires en 2025 contre 44,7 % en 2019 ; les détections d’E. coli producteurs de carbapénémase sont de plus en plus fréquentes en milieu communautaire. Les infections sanguines dues à des souches d’E. coli résistantes aux céphalosporines de troisième génération ont augmenté de 16,4 %, et seuls cinq pays ont atteint leurs objectifs nationaux en 2025. – Source : BEACON, EU/EEA : Rising carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae and E. coli bloodstream infections threaten 2030 AMR targets et Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales - fourth update, pages consultées le 24 novembre 2026.

Diphtérie

• Australie : Le point de situation national daté du 16 novembre 2026 fait état de 653 cas de diphtérie signalés en 2026, dont un cas probable, contre une moyenne de 17 cas pour la même période entre 2022 et 2025. Quatorze cas ont été signalés au cours de la dernière quinzaine, contre 12 au cours de la quinzaine précédente : 7 en Australie-Occidentale, 5 dans le Territoire du Nord, 1 en Australie-Méridionale et 1 dans le Queensland, dont 4 cas de diphtérie respiratoire. L’activité reste inférieure au pic intervenu entre fin mai et début juin 2026. Depuis le 1er janvier, des cas ont été recensés dans le Territoire du Nord (336), en Australie-Occidentale (287), en Australie-Méridionale (24) et dans le Queensland (6) ; tous les cas autochtones appartiennent au même groupe génomique. Les Aborigènes et/ou les Insulaires du détroit de Torres représentent 95,3 % des cas, et 88,9 % des cas autochtones vivent dans des zones reculées ou très reculées. Deux tiers des cas (66,3 %) sont cutanés et 30,8 % sont respiratoires. Au total, 120 personnes (18,4 % des cas) ont été hospitalisées et un décès a été signalé en avril 2026. – Source : Australian Centre for Disease Control, Diphtheria in Australia, epidemiological update as at 16 November 2026, page consultée le 24 novembre 2026.

Maladies respiratoires

• Monde : Le 19 novembre 2026, le Groupe consultatif technique sur l’évolution du virus SARS-CoV-2 (TAG-VE) de l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé (OMS) a qualifié le variant PJ.2.1 du SARS-CoV-2 de « variant sous surveillance », indiquant que le risque supplémentaire pour la santé publique était faible au niveau mondial. Issu de la lignée JN.1, ce variant a été détecté pour la première fois dans la province canadienne de l’Ontario, en mai 2026. Il a ensuite progressé, passant de 1,0 % des séquences analysées au cours de la semaine 33 à 11,6 % au cours de la semaine 41. Ces pourcentages ont été établis sur la base de 722 séquences transmises par 18 pays au 8 novembre 2026. items.title: From Village Gatherings to Beachside Book Talks: How To Pick Your Perfect Lit Fest This Winter
items.blurb: If your idea of a good weekend involves listening to a favourite author, discovering new books or spending hours discussing stories, the next two months offer plenty to look forward to. India's winter literature festival season gets underway today, 27 November, with events opening in Dehradun and Lucknow. Seven more festivals are scheduled across December and January, giving book lovers plenty of time to plan a trip. But how do you choose the one that suits you? In January 2025, Nisha Retnamma, an author living in the UAE, flew to Kozhikode for the Kerala Literature Festival because it let her "meet and listen to all your favourite authors from across the world". Keep her test in mind: whose voices do you most want to hear? Which voices are you here for? Start with language. If you want to hear writers in Hindi, Urdu and other Indian languages, head to Koshala from 27 to 30 November 2026, where live mushairas , kavi sammelans and translation studies fill the programme, and tickets start at Rs 100 on BookMyShow. From poetry under open skies to conversations by the coast, literature festivals turn reading into shared experiences. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) If you are curious about languages you rarely hear, wait for the Hyderabad Literary Festival, from 22 to 24 January 2027, at Sattva Knowledge City. Sessions on indigenous and endangered languages sit beside a poetry stream called Kaavya Dhaara , and entry is free. Jaipur also devotes a Bhasha Swarmala series to India's languages in its 20th edition. Do you want a crowd, the sea or quiet? Prefer a crowd? Join the Jaipur Literature Festival , from 14 to 18 January 2027, at Hotel Clarks Amer. Jaipur resident Rohit Mathur, who loves attending such events, says, "The global presence of Jaipur excites me", and the programme gives him plenty to chase, from debates with prize-winning authors to pop-up bookshops and evening concerts. General registration starts at Rs 200, and students pay Rs 100 for all five days. Want the sea? The Kerala Literature Festival , from 21 to 24 January on Kozhikode Beach, marks its tenth edition with Australia as its guest nation, and the waves soften the crowd. Author Martin Goodman, who attended in 2026, enjoyed being able to "breeze into conversation beneath a crescent moon", although two sessions he turned up for were cancelled. Keep a backup in mind. A good literary gathering can take place anywhere, from a bustling city hotel to a quiet village. Photograph: ( Experiential Marketing ) English literature student Athira Gopinath says she would not miss it at any price. Delegate registration is free online. Want quiet? Wayanad, from 20 to 23 December, is held in a gram panchayat rather than a city, with campfire readings and a heritage walk among its signature events. Novelist KR Meera, who has attended many festivals in big cities, predicted before its first edition that the "participation of the local people is going to be unique". The biennial event drew over 110,000 visitors in 2024, and a one-day adult ticket costs Rs 50. The festival's own website lists 19 December as the start, so confirm before you book. How do you like to listen? The Bangalore Literature Festival's 15th edition, from 11 to 13 December at Freedom Park, a former colonial jail, is free with online registration. Bindu Manoj, who has attended since the festival began, felt after the 2017 edition that the early years were "the best with more literature", so read each programme before you commit. items.title: How a Football Tournament in Nagaland Brought 30 Villages Together to Ban Pangolin Hunting
items.blurb: On 24 November 2026, Ngoushutho Ngouri spotted an unusual animal crossing a road near a residential area in Meluri, Nagaland. It was a Chinese pangolin, a critically endangered mammal threatened by hunting and the illegal wildlife trade. Ngouri alerted forest officials, who rushed to the spot, examined the animal and found it healthy and uninjured. The pangolin was safely released into a forest habitat away from human settlements. Just weeks earlier, the local community had come together over a shared love for football and made a collective decision to protect this very animal. Across Nagaland, Manipur and Gujarat, similar efforts are showing how everyday decisions by residents, village leaders, farmers and fishers can help protect some of the world's most threatened species. A football tournament with a purpose In October 2026, eight football clubs from neighbouring villages came together in Nagaland for a rather unusual sporting event: the Pangolin Cup. Organised by the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) , in collaboration with the Meluri Range Sports Association and the Nagaland Forest Department, the six-day tournament attracted at least 10,000 participants and spectators. Between the excitement of football matches, residents learnt about pangolins, why they are hunted for their meat and scales, and how these animals help maintain forest ecosystems by feeding on ants and termites. What followed went well beyond the football field. The Pochury Hoho, the apex leadership body of the Pochury Naga community, passed a resolution banning pangolin hunting across 30 villages. Anyone found hunting or trading the animal would face a fine of Rs 50,000. Weeks later, Ngouri's decision to alert forest officials offered a tangible example of how such awareness could translate into action. A football tournament in Nagaland helped bring communities together to protect the critically endangered Chinese pangolin. Photograph: (Wildlife Trust of India (WTI)) Over 300 villages unite to protect pangolins Elsewhere in Nagaland, village councils are using traditional systems of governance to protect wildlife. In February 2026, the United Sangtam Likhum Pumji, the apex body representing the Sangtam Naga community, banned pangolin hunting across 42 villages in Kiphire district. Following months of discussions with conservationists, village councils took responsibility for enforcing the ban, with violations handled by customary courts. As reported by Mongabay , such resolutions are helping communities use their customary laws to protect endangered wildlife. Neighbouring Manipur has seen similar efforts. In August 2024, the Tangkhul Naga Awunga Long, the apex body representing the Tangkhul Naga community, signed a resolution banning pangolin hunting and consumption across 230 villages . In April 2025, when farmers discovered a Chinese pangolin in farmland near Tangkhul Khullen village, they informed community leader Kashung Tennyson. The animal was subsequently rescued and released into the wild. Together, these three community resolutions cover more than 300 villages, bringing local residents and traditional institutions into the fight against wildlife trafficking. Fishers who cut their nets to save whale sharks Thousands of kilometres away, along Gujarat’s coast, another community is helping protect the world's largest fish. Until the early 2000s, whale sharks were hunted along the Gujarat coast for their fins, liver oil, skin and meat. In 2004, WTI launched a conservation initiative in partnership with the Gujarat Forest Department and Tata Chemicals, working with fishing communities to raise awareness about the endangered species. Over the years, fishers began voluntarily releasing whale sharks that accidentally became entangled in their fishing nets. Some even cut their expensive nets to free the animals, with a compensation programme helping cover their financial losses. According to WTI, Gujarat’s fishing communities have helped release 1,042 adult whale sharks and 22 young ones. In November 2026, these communities received national recognition from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for their contribution to whale shark conservation. The initiative has also expanded to Kerala, Lakshadweep and Goa, where fishers are being trained to recognise and safely release whale sharks. Gujarat’s fishing communities have voluntarily helped release over 1,000 whale sharks caught in fishing nets. Photograph: (Wildlife Trust of India) For a resident walking along a village road, a farmer working in his field or a fisher heading out to sea, an unexpected encounter with an endangered animal can become an opportunity to save its life. By bringing conservation into their sports , traditions, livelihoods and everyday decisions, these communities are showing how ordinary citizens can play a meaningful role in protecting India's wildlife.

items.title: 6 Indian Childhood Games to Get Your Kids Moving, Laughing & Off Screens This Winter Break
items.blurb: “Just five more minutes!” If you've ever tried getting a child to put down a phone or tablet, chances are you've heard this familiar refrain. But long before cartoons were available at the tap of a screen and games came with colourful animations, childhood entertainment looked a little different. It meant chalk-drawn squares on the floor, marbles tucked into pockets, endless rounds of hide-and-seek and friends gathering in the neighbourhood until someone called them home. The best part? Most of these games needed little more than a few friends, some open space and a generous dose of imagination. Bringing these old-school games back can be a fun way to encourage children to take a break from screens, get moving and spend quality time with others. Here are six Indian childhood favourites worth introducing to the next generation. 1. Hopscotch ( Stapu ) All you need is a piece of chalk and a little space to get started. Draw a series of numbered boxes on the ground, toss a small stone into one of them and ask children to hop through the squares on one foot, skipping the box containing the stone. A chalk-drawn square, a few friends and a game of hopscotch can turn an ordinary afternoon into hours of fun. Photograph: ( Adobe Stock ) Known as stapu in many parts of India, hopscotch is a simple game that can keep children entertained for hours. It encourages balance, coordination and concentration, while giving them a chance to cheer each other on. 2. Seven Stones ( Lagori ) A game that brings together teamwork, speed and a little strategy, lagori is a favourite that deserves a comeback. Stack seven flat stones on top of one another and divide the players into two teams. One team tries to knock down the stack with a ball, while the other attempts to rebuild it before getting hit by the ball. The opposing team tries to stop them by tagging players with the ball. Seven Stones, or Lagori, brings children together for a game of teamwork, quick thinking and friendly competition. Photograph: (AI generated) The game gets everyone running, dodging, planning and laughing. It is also a wonderful way to introduce children to teamwork and friendly competition. 3. Carrom Rainy afternoon? Too hot to play outside? Bring out the carrom board! This classic indoor game needs a board, striker and carrom coins. Players take turns flicking the striker to pocket their coins, aiming to clear the board before their opponents. Carrom is a timeless indoor favourite that brings generations together over a little strategy and plenty of laughter. Photograph: ( iStock ) Carrom is a lovely way to bring the family together. It helps children practise hand-eye coordination, patience and strategic thinking. Parents can even make it a family tournament, complete with playful challenges and a little friendly rivalry. 4. Tip-Cat ( Gilli-Danda ) Think of it as a traditional Indian game that puts hand-eye coordination to the test. Gilli-danda uses two wooden sticks: a small tapered one (the gilli ) and a longer one (the danda ). With just two wooden sticks and some open space, gilli-danda introduces children to a game enjoyed by generations before smartphones. Photograph: ( Channapatna Toys ) Players use the longer stick to flick the smaller one into the air and then hit it as far as possible. The game can be played in an open ground with simple rules agreed upon by everyone. It is a wonderful way for children to enjoy outdoor play, practise coordination and discover a game that entertained generations before smartphones existed. 5. King, Minister, Thief, Soldier (Raja, Mantri, Chor, Sipahi) This is a fun indoor game that needs just four players and a few small slips of paper. Write the names Raja , Mantri , Chor and Sipahi on four slips and distribute them among the players. The person who gets Raja reveals their identity, while the others have to figure out who the Chor is. The Mantri gets a chance to guess, and the Sipahi can help with the investigation, depending on the rules the group decides. With guessing, suspense and plenty of laughter, this game can turn an ordinary afternoon into a mini detective adventure. 6. Tag and Chase ( Kho-Kho ) A playground favourite, kho-kho is a fast-paced team game that keeps children on their toes. Two teams take turns chasing and dodging. Players from the chasing team sit in a row, facing alternate directions, while one active chaser tries to tag opponents. By calling ' kho ' and transferring the chase to a teammate, players must think quickly and move strategically. From chasing friends across a playground to drawing squares on the floor, traditional games make movement and imagination part of everyday childhood. Photograph: ( Dsource ) Besides being a great way to get children running, kho-kho encourages teamwork, agility and quick decision-making. Making room for play The idea isn't to ban screens altogether or make children feel guilty about enjoying their favourite digital games. Instead, it is about making space for other kinds of fun, too. Parents can start small by setting aside 20–30 minutes for a family game, inviting neighbourhood children over for an afternoon of outdoor play or teaching their little ones a game they enjoyed growing up. After all, childhood doesn't always need a screen, a scorecard or a fancy toy. Sometimes, all it takes is a chalk-drawn square, a few friends and the freedom to play. items.title: ‘I Want My Own Home’: Trans Actor Jeeva on Finding Her Place in Tamil Cinema & Making It to Toronto
items.blurb: At 13, Jeeva Subramanian arrived in Chennai with Rs 300 her mother had given her. Her brother had accompanied her to the city, but left her at Koyambedu bus stand. Unfamiliar with the place and with nowhere else to go, she waited for him to return. “I did not know anyone in Chennai. I thought my brother would come back to take me, so I kept waiting in the same place. I would go to the public toilet, wash myself and my clothes, and return to where I had been sitting. I kept thinking he would look for me there,” she recalls. Two days passed before Jeeva realised that he was not coming back. By then, she had spent nearly three days at the bus stand. A woman who worked there cleaning the premises eventually approached her and offered to find her a job. That conversation led to Jeeva’s first job in Chennai, at a shop inside the bus stand. She earned Rs 40 a day, with food and accommodation provided by the employer, though her wages were held back for seven days at a time. At 13, Jeeva waited two days at Koyambedu before accepting her brother would not return. Photograph: (Instagram/ @jeeva_subramaniam.offl ) “I was only 13. That was my first job in Chennai . They gave us food and a place to stay, so I continued working,” she says. The job lasted about two months. When it ended, the bus stand became her refuge again. She slept within sight of a police booth because she felt safer there, and took up whatever work she could find, including carrying vegetables at the Koyambedu market in the early hours of the morning. At the time, Jeeva knew she was a girl, but did not know what it meant to be transgender or that there was a community of people like her. “I lived with the feeling that I was a girl. I did not know there was a transgender community. I was a child. I did not understand what was happening around me,” she says. From surviving to finding her place Jeeva eventually found work clearing used banana leaves after wedding functions at a marriage hall. But workers were asked to leave once a wedding was over, and she was again left searching for somewhere safe to stay. A visitor at one of the functions gave her a contact for a housekeeping company. Through it, she found work at a sweets outlet in Vadapalani, earning Rs 2,200 a month, along with food and accommodation. Around this period, Jeeva began to understand her identity and gradually encountered other transgender people. Dance offered another possibility . She joined a dance school and began performing at programmes, sometimes wearing wigs for devotional and glamour songs. When the programmes stopped, she was once again left looking for work. A friend helped her find occasional performances, but that too came to an end when he moved to Dubai. On Dharma Durai’s set, Vijay Sethupathi’s warm embrace gave Jeeva the courage to continue acting. Her next opening came through cinema, where she began working as a touch-up assistant. She had already developed an interest in acting, but expressing that ambition was not easy. People questioned whether she was good-looking enough to act, and once they learnt she was transgender, some became reluctant to employ her. “I used to tell people that I wanted to act, but they would ask me, ‘What are you going to do by acting? Are you beautiful enough?’ They would dismiss the idea. After they found out that I was trans, people became hesitant to take me for work. Some of the other assistants would keep teasing me,” she says. There were, however, people who stood up for her. Actor Bala Singh, with whom she worked for several years, was particularly protective. Jeeva remembers him telling others, “She is my daughter. Why are you talking about her like that?” She also worked with actors including Anushka Shetty, Taapsee Pannu, Shriya, and Ramya Nambesan. Actor Shriya encouraged her to learn makeup, a skill that could support her financially. Jeeva went on to work as a bridal makeup artist , doing makeup for around 400 brides. But discrimination followed her into this profession too, and a bad experience eventually forced her to give it up. Jeeva created Dorothy’s look herself, gaining 13 kilograms and sending photographs to convince the filmmakers. Photograph: (AI-Generated collage) Even as she found ways to earn, the search for a stable home remained unresolved. The rooms she could afford were often in poor condition, with rainwater entering the house and collecting up to her knees. The 2015 Chennai floods damaged her home and left her with very little. A friend, Sheela, took her in and gave her food and shelter. These experiences had already taught Jeeva how precarious everyday life could be. But it was on a film set that she encountered a moment of acceptance that would change how she saw her place in the industry. The embrace that changed her relationship with cinema By the time she was called to work on Dharma Durai , Jeeva was considering leaving Chennai. She had worked for years, tried different jobs and felt that none of it was taking her anywhere. She accepted the opportunity partly because she admired actor Radhika. The shoot, however, was difficult. People in the crowd used slurs against her, and she found it hard to continue performing. She broke down and cried. Actor Vijay Sethupathi noticed what was happening, intervened, and asked the crowd to stop. He told them, “She is my younger sister,” before hugging Jeeva and kissing her forehead. For someone who had experienced rejection and abuse, the gesture carried a meaning that went far beyond the film set. “An embrace may be a normal thing for other people, but it did not come to me so easily. I cannot even put into words what I felt that day. When he hugged me, I closed my eyes for a moment, and it felt as though the whole universe was spinning around me. Nobody had hugged me like that before. He kissed me on the forehead, and I held on to him and cried,” she says. Her short film won 58 awards, yet recognition did not guarantee steady work or housing. Director Seenu Ramasamy then encouraged her to continue with the scene, telling her that the very people insulting her should one day whistle and applaud when they saw her on screen. “He could have said that they should get someone else to do the scene. Instead, he told me to act with confidence. That gave me the courage to go back and perform. That is the magic of Dharma Durai for me,” she says. The film was released in 2016, and Jeeva began to be recognised by people who had seen her on screen. Her father, too, called her “my daughter”, a moment she remembers with particular happiness. But the recognition did not translate into a steady livelihood. People who had earlier hired her as an assistant began to see her only as an actor and stopped calling her for makeup work. “I had to start running around for work all over again. Earlier, at least I was working as an assistant. After the film, people would say, ‘You have become an actor. How can we call you for assistant work?’ Nobody called me. I struggled ten times more than I had before. There were days when I could not find food. I would go to the Vadapalani temple and eat the food they distributed. I even went to Hyderabad and stayed in a small lodge, calling actors and asking them to take me on as a makeup assistant so I could pay my rent,” she says. After neighbours objected, a landlord returned the ₹40,000 advance Jeeva had paid for a house. Photograph: (Deccan Chronicle) Being visible on screen, she realised, did not necessarily mean being accepted off it. Jeeva continued looking for work, taking up roles in films and short films. One of her short films went on to win 58 awards, while her work brought her opportunities in projects including Airaa , Darbar and Suzhal . But she did not want recognition to be mistaken for charity. She wanted opportunities to demonstrate her ability, and that determination would be tested again when she auditioned for Dorothy . Proving what she could do in Dorothy When the team behind Dorothy approached Jeeva, they initially felt she looked too young for the character. They were looking for someone older and heavier. Jeeva, who weighed around 64 kg, decided to gain weight and shape the character’s appearance herself. She gained 13 kg, choosing a cotton saree, double nose studs, a bun and grey hair to complete the look. She took photographs of herself and sent them to the team. “I told them, ‘Give me one opportunity. Only if you give me a chance can I prove myself.’ I wanted them to see that I could do the character. I put together the look, took the photographs myself and sent them. I was determined to get this opportunity,” she says. Jeeva also performed the physically demanding sequences herself, without a body double. During one sequence, she was hurt, and actor Karthi helped her up and checked on her. When the crew applauded her performance, he came over and hugged her. “He came running and hugged me tightly. He even helped me because I had been hurt. I felt that same kind of embrace I had received years ago during Dharma Durai ,” she says. Jeeva’s Diwali cake marked celebration after years of spending the festival alone behind closed doors. Photograph: (Still from Dorothy) The film became another turning point. At a rough-cut screening, Jeeva was moved by what she saw and hugged director Karthik Subbaraj. He told her they would take the film to Canada. At the Toronto International Film Festival in 2026, she experienced a warm welcome from people who had watched her work. Actor Rajinikanth also praised her performance. Yet, even as her work travelled beyond India and more people began recognising her, the difficulties she faced away from the camera did not disappear. In fact, being more recognisable sometimes made finding a house even harder. The struggle to find a home continues Jeeva has been searching for a house for around six months. A property that would ordinarily be rented for Rs 10,000 has been quoted to her at Rs 30,000. She once paid an advance of Rs 40,000 for a house, only for the landlord to return the money after neighbours objected to a transgender woman moving into their street. The questions she faces from brokers and landlords are often invasive. They ask how many people will visit her, whether she intends to bring clients home, and how many people she will bring in each day. In one instance, a broker suggested that she would have to pay far beyond the advertised rent. Jeeva has also been told that a house could be rented to her only if a male acquaintance signed the agreement, because the landlord did not trust her on her own. “I have been looking for a house for six months. If a house normally costs Rs 10,000, they tell me it will cost Rs 30,000. I paid Rs 40,000 as an advance for one house, and then the people in that street said that a transgender person should not be allowed to live there. They told the owner to return my advance. This is what keeps happening,” she says. Beyond international applause for Dorothy, Jeeva hopes for a 400-square-foot home where she can rest. She recalls being asked questions that implied she was offering sexual services. When she explained that she went to work and could pay only what she earned, she was told not to pretend to be poor. A transgender woman who approached the same broker was quoted Rs 35,000 and managed to secure a house, Jeeva says, making her feel that access to housing can depend on how much a landlord believes a person can pay. The uncertainty has affected her daily life. Her belongings have been packed and unpacked repeatedly as brokers promise that a house will be confirmed the next day. She has kept much of her household packed for months and says she has cried after conversations with people who were supposed to help her find a place. Jeeva has also approached the government for assistance. She says she was once told that a house could be allotted to her, but the property was around 50 km away, making it impractical for her work. When she sought an allocation closer to the city, she was told that housing categories had specific allocations for several communities but no separate percentage for transgender applicants. She is now trying to secure an appointment with the minister to submit a formal request. Jeeva wants neither charity nor special treatment; she wants affordable housing and dignity without interrogation. “I do not want anyone to give me a house for free. If I have to pay Rs 4 lakh or Rs 5 lakh, I am willing to do that. Just allot me a small house. I have faced so many things in life, but I have cried more over this house problem than over many of the other things that happened to me. Every time I go to look at a house, the questions people ask me are so humiliating. I do not even know how to answer them,” she says. She has a simple request: “I want a small house of around 400 square feet, a house that is mine. I do not want to keep proving to people that I am a good person, that I am respectable, or explaining where I am going and what work I do. I just want to sleep peacefully in my own house.” The contrast is difficult to ignore. Jeeva has appeared on screens watched by audiences across countries, received appreciation from some of Tamil cinema’s most prominent names and represented a community that rarely gets such visibility. Yet she is still made to answer questions about whether she can be trusted with a rental home. A celebration, and a wish for ordinary life The difference between being seen and being allowed to live freely is something Jeeva has experienced in smaller, everyday ways too. She recalls that, in earlier years, Diwali was not a festival she celebrated with others. She would buy enough rice and lentils to last a few days, shut the doors and keep to herself. After Dorothy , she decided to mark the festival differently. She bought a cake and cut it for Diwali. Jeeva’s journey is a testament to finding her voice, claiming her place and rewriting what representation can look like. “It may seem like a small thing, but it gave me so much happiness,” she says. For Jeeva, the cake was not simply a festive purchase. It was a moment in which she allowed herself to celebrate, rather than spend the day withdrawing from the world. It was also a reminder that the life she wants is not defined only by film roles, awards or public recognition. It includes the ordinary freedoms that many people take for granted: a secure place to return to, the ability to celebrate without fear and the dignity of not having to explain herself to strangers. She continues to look for work and a home, while hoping that the attention around Dorothy will lead to more opportunities. She would like to win a National Award one day. But when she speaks about what she wants beyond cinema, her wish is strikingly modest. After years of being pushed out of homes, workplaces and public spaces, Jeeva is asking for a place where she can close the door at the end of the day and rest without having to prove that she belongs there. The applause may follow her from one theatre to another, but what she is still waiting for is a home of her own.

items.title: Trump is destroying the rule of law in the US – to protect himself and the tech titans he worships as new gods | Jonathan Freedland
items.blurb:
To get Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, the president trampled on the justice system, national security and the trust America needs to do business in the global economy

Don’t let the sex distract you. Or the lies or the boardroom intrigue or even the AI-generated bra, all of which could have come from an especially wild episode of Succession. Don’t let that lure you into thinking that the Jensen Huang affair is, as Donald Trump would have it, little more than a sex scandal involving a corporate maestro. It is much more serious than that. The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law.

It can be hard to see that through the thicket of questions that surround this episode, each one of which, don’t get me wrong, merits attention. Consider the personal profit Trump made thanks to his re-installation of Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, the world’s leading maker of advanced AI chips. Breaking the norm observed by previous presidents who, keen to avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, either divested themselves of stock holdings or placed them in a blind trust, Trump cheerfully buys and sells stocks in companies whose fates he can influence. He saw the value of his shares in Nvidia plunge when Huang was forced out, following revelations that the CEO had had an affair with Alice Huang, reportedly an asset of Chinese intelligence. Last weekend Trump urged the board to reconsider; Huang was reinstated on Monday and Nvidia’s value promptly soared – putting $15m in Trump’s pocket. Not for the first time, he had used the power of his office to enrich himself.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

He’s perennially disgraced and yet he just won’t go away – now he’s joined the latest Brexit debate. Isn’t there a mute button, or an exile plan that really works?

What a week it has been for Indispensable Men. In the old days, if someone were forced to resign, whether as ambassador to Washington or boss of a trillion-dollar company, they would become what we quaintly used to call “disgraced”. Perhaps they would spend the rest of their days volunteering with a charity. Certainly, for a good decade afterwards, they would acquire the journalistic epithet “shamed” on first mention. Later – much later – they might be allowed back into public life, in some lesser role where they could be discreetly supervised, to check exactly how many emails they were sending to which people arranging what holidays.

But what’s this we find over on news website UnHerd? Why, it’s a 2,000-word essay from one Peter Mandelson on the difficulties of rejoining the European Union. Mandelson … Mandelson. That name definitely rings a bell. Let’s see if there’s a clue at the bottom of the piece. Ah, yes: “Peter Mandelson is a former cabinet minister and EU Trade Commissioner.” That’s the chap: Gordon Brown’s former business secretary. Though I feel as if I’ve seen his name in the news a bit more recently than 2010. Might he be a “former” anything else?

items.title: The most surprising thing about Burnham’s slow politics is this: it could be working | Andy Beckett
items.blurb:
‘Andy time’ may frustrate the media and voters impatient for change – but after years of short premierships and rushed policies, isn’t this the reset Westminster needs?

Andy Burnham is making a lot of people impatient. Political journalists, pro-EU activists, climate campaigners, fossil-fuel lobbyists, recipients of welfare benefits, advocates of welfare cuts, enemies of neoliberalism, enthusiasts for renationalisation, members of the armed forces and even cabinet colleagues: all are waiting for the prime minister to make big decisions, and thus reveal the true nature of his administration, four months after its beginning.

Since his Manchester mayoralty, some of Burnham’s co-workers have had a phrase for his tendency to take things at his own tempo: “Andy time”. He lets interesting conversations overrun, likes to ponder issues without being rushed, and pushes back crucial announcements. The unveiling of his 10-year plan – a typically ambitious but loose Burnham timespan, and one of his government’s pivotal moments – has been repeatedly delayed. According to the website Politico, it has been pencilled in for 17 December, the final day of the parliamentary calendar.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist
